title: A war poem flagged as incitement
scenario: Moderation lead Oksana Melnyk at a regional social platform in Ukraine reviews an appeal. A well-known poet posted a verse celebrating fallen soldiers, which the automated filter removed as glorifying violence. The poem has been shared by thousands of grieving families, and its removal sparked outrage. Other users have posted nearly identical verses with calls to attack named civilians, and the filter cannot reliably tell them apart. Oksana has a small team and an hour before the poet's supporters plan a public campaign. She must decide whether to restore the post and how to handle similar ones.
options: Restore the poem and add a human review step for all poetry flagged by the filter, accepting slower responses to genuine incitement.
Keep the removal for now and ask the poet to repost with context, preserving a consistent rule against glorifying violence.
Restore the poem and loosen the filter's glorification category overall, accepting that some harmful posts will stay up longer.
tension: expression and grief vs. preventing incitement

title: Reclaimed slurs in a queer community forum
scenario: Volunteer administrator Thabo Nkosi runs an online forum for LGBTQ+ people across Southern Africa. A slur-detection tool automatically hides posts containing certain words, but members use some of them affectionately among themselves, and removing them frustrates many. Others in the community, particularly older members, find the words wounding and say they make the forum unsafe. Outsiders have occasionally joined to harass, using the same words. Thabo does not have the resources to review every post manually. A heated discussion is under way and he needs to adjust the filter settings tonight.
options: Switch off the automatic hiding for verified long-term members and keep it for new accounts, accepting that harm to older members may continue.
Keep the filter strict for everyone, accepting that members' reclaimed usage will be removed and some will leave.
Replace the filter with a community flagging system where members decide together, accepting slower action on abusive posts.

title: Medical misinformation during the cholera outbreak
scenario: Trust and safety manager Nusrat Jahan at a messaging platform popular in Bangladesh finds a viral voice message claiming that a herbal drink cures cholera and that rehydration salts are a government poison plot. Health officials say people are delaying treatment. The message is spread across thousands of private groups, so removing it requires either breaking encryption or limiting message forwarding for all users. A forwarding limit would hinder legitimate emergency alerts too. Local officials urgently ask her to act and she has a few hours before the next wave of rainfall worsens conditions.
options: Restrict forwarding to one chat at a time across the country for a fixed period, accepting disruption to legitimate warnings.
Send a pinned counter-message from health authorities to all users and leave forwarding unchanged, respecting private communication.
Add a warning label to forwarded messages that match known false health claims, acknowledging that scanning content for the matches raises privacy concerns.

title: A government takedown order on election eve
scenario: Country policy director Mehmet Aksoy at a global video platform receives a legal order from a government to remove a documentary alleging corruption by the ruling party, two days before a close election. The order is formally valid under local law. Non-compliance could lead to the platform being blocked nationwide, cutting off millions of users including independent journalists. Compliance would silence a film that is probably accurate but has not been independently verified. The company has not decided on a standard approach. Mehmet is the senior decision-maker in the country and must respond in twelve hours.
options: Comply by geo-blocking the film within the country, publish the order transparently, and appeal through the courts.
Refuse to remove the film and accept the possibility of a nationwide block of the platform for all users.
Remove the film temporarily while seeking an urgent court review, restoring it quickly if the order is found unlawful.

title: The children's channel with disturbing cartoons
scenario: Content reviewer Delphine Moreau at a French streaming platform finds a popular channel making cartoons in which familiar children's characters are shown in distressing situations. Technically none of the videos breaks the rules: no gore, no explicit content. Parents' groups are complaining that children are upset, but the channel's creator, a teenager in a small town, argues it is dark comedy meant for older viewers and mislabelled by the algorithm's recommendations. The channel supports his family. Delphine can restrict the channel, take no action, or recommend changes. A parents' petition arrives on Friday.
options: Age-restrict the content and remove it from children's recommendations while leaving it available to older viewers.
Take no action, since the content does not violate any stated rule and parents hold responsibility for what children watch.
Demonetise the channel and demand a rewrite of its titles and thumbnails, pressuring the creator while avoiding removal.

title: Terror footage in a journalist's archive
scenario: Archive manager Yasmin Haddad at an independent Syrian-diaspora documentation group, hosted on a major cloud video service, is told the service's automated system removed dozens of videos showing attacks on civilians as terrorist content. They are evidence for future war-crimes investigations and many cannot be recovered elsewhere. The service's policy cannot easily distinguish documentation from propaganda. A human appeal is possible but may take weeks, and legal processes are approaching deadlines. Yasmin must decide how to respond, knowing the videos also show identifiable victims whose families have not consented to publication.
options: File mass appeals and mobilise legal and press pressure to restore the videos quickly, prioritising preservation of evidence.
Quietly restore the archive from backups to a private evidence repository shared only with investigators, abandoning public hosting.
Restore selected videos with faces blurred, pending consent from families, accepting some loss of evidentiary value.

title: Shouting match in the Sinhala-language comments
scenario: Moderation contractor Chamari Wickramasinghe in Colombo is the only reviewer fluent in the local language and dialect for a large platform, which relies on translation software for the rest. After a communal clash, the comments under news posts fill with threats, but the machine translator mislabels harmless banter as hate and misses coded threats. She is handling several thousand flagged items per day and exhausted. She is allowed to suggest a rule change to her supervisor in another country, who rarely replies quickly. Tensions in the city are rising.
options: Recommend temporarily disabling comments on news posts about the clash, preventing threats but silencing ordinary discussion.
Recommend hiring more language-qualified reviewers, accepting that it will take weeks while the tension continues.
Recommend automatically hiding every flagged comment until reviewed, accepting that many harmless ones will be hidden temporarily.

title: A grieving mother's memorial page and a hate group
scenario: Community manager Ibrahim Sesay at a West African social app is asked by a woman to keep the memorial page of her murdered son online. A hate group has begun posting abusive comments there and falsely claiming the son was a criminal. The page contains private photos and condolences from hundreds of people. Limiting comments would protect her but cut off mourners, and the platform's rules don't allow locking pages on request. Deleting the page would erase a memorial she treasures. Ibrahim has discretion to apply exceptions but must record his reasons.
options: Lock comments to approved followers only and ban the abusive accounts, making an exception to the standard rule.
Delete the abusive comments individually as they appear, following the normal rules and keeping the page open.
Convert the page into a read-only tribute with no comments, preserving the memorial but ending public mourning interactions.
tension: open mourning vs. protection from abuse

title: Satire of the king and the lese-majeste law
scenario: Legal counsel Napat Srisai at a regional forum platform in Bangkok receives a complaint that a user's cartoon mocking the monarchy violates the country's lese-majeste law, punishable by years in prison for the poster and potentially for staff who knowingly host such content. The cartoon is widely shared among students and appears to be political satire. The company has local employees who could face criminal liability. Withdrawing the content protects staff but contributes to repression; leaving it up risks arrest. Napat must give the company's leadership a recommendation by tonight.
options: Remove the cartoon in the country, notify the poster of the legal demand, and publish the removal in a transparency report.
Leave the cartoon online, move local staff out of the country if needed, and accept the legal and business consequences.
Ask the poster whether they would prefer the platform to remove it, giving them the choice about their own risk.

title: Deepfake porn takedown speed versus due process
scenario: Safety engineer Marguerite Dubois-Lang at a Canadian image-hosting service is designing a system for victims to report intimate images generated without consent. A fast automatic takedown would protect victims quickly, but past systems were abused by people falsely reporting legitimate photographs of rivals, activists and journalists. Verification takes days, during which an image may spread widely. She must choose how much proof to require before the system removes an image, knowing that either error harms real people and that the product launch is next month.
options: Remove reported images instantly and restore them if the poster successfully contests the claim, accepting that some false reports will cause temporary removals.
Require identity verification from the reporter before removal, accepting a delay of a day or more for each case.
Remove instantly only when automated detection finds a high-confidence match, sending uncertain cases to human review.
tension: victim protection vs. protection from false reports

title: Teaching the history of a massacre
scenario: Community volunteer Hasan Demirci moderates a Kurdish-language history channel, which a platform's automated system keeps flagging for violent imagery in photos of a historical massacre used in education. The images are disturbing yet central to the community's remembrance and are denied by some authorities. Lifting the restriction requires a special educational exemption that the platform grants rarely. A rival group has begun mass-reporting the channel in the hope of having it removed. Hasan can blur the images, add warnings, or seek the exemption, which would require disclosing his identity, which could be dangerous.
options: Apply for the educational exemption using his real identity, accepting personal risk to protect the unblurred historical record.
Blur the images and add content warnings, keeping the channel active and preserving the originals elsewhere.
Move the archive off the platform to a self-hosted site, reducing exposure to mass-reporting but reaching a much smaller audience.

title: Moderating a livestream in real time
scenario: Live operations moderator Pita Havili, working a night shift for a Pacific streaming service, sees a young man livestreaming from a cliff top, saying he intends to end his life. Hundreds are watching and commenting, some urging him on. Platform protocol says to contact emergency services and not interrupt the stream if a crisis team is engaged, but the crisis team is unreachable for several minutes. Cutting the stream could remove the only way to locate him and might escalate his distress. Pita has a few moments to decide what to do.
options: Leave the stream running, delete abusive comments, and send the location data to emergency services and local police at once.
Cut the stream to stop the audience seeing the situation, and send the location details to emergency services.
Keep the stream running and post a supportive message from the platform, directing the man to a crisis line while emergency services are alerted.
tension: preventing harm to the person vs. protecting viewers

title: A political party's youth wing and coordinated hashtags
scenario: Integrity analyst Rodrigo Estevez at a Mexican social network detects thousands of accounts posting identical messages attacking a journalist who reported on cartel links. Many accounts are real young people who were given scripted posts by a party youth wing in exchange for small rewards. The messages themselves contain insults but no explicit threats. Removing all the accounts would be seen as political censorship, while leaving them might expose the journalist to escalating harassment and real danger. His team has a policy on coordinated behaviour but has never applied it against a major party.
options: Apply the coordinated behaviour policy and remove the networked posts, publishing a clear public explanation.
Reduce the reach of the coordinated posts without removing them, and offer the journalist enhanced protection tools.
Take no action against the accounts, since the posts are individual political speech, but provide the journalist with security support.
tension: protecting a journalist vs. political neutrality
coordinated inauthentic behaviour vs. real participants

title: Religious criticism in a conservative community
scenario: Platform trust officer Zainab Idris in Kano reviews a post by a university lecturer who criticises a prominent cleric's interpretation of religious texts. Hundreds of reports say it is blasphemous, and a crowd has gathered outside the lecturer's home in response to screenshots circulating elsewhere. The post is polite and academic in tone. Removing it might calm the crowd but would suggest the platform enforces blasphemy norms. Keeping it up may fuel violence. She has the authority to act now but is aware that decisions made in this case will be quoted for years.
options: Keep the post online, contact local authorities to protect the lecturer, and publish the platform's reasoning.
Hide the post temporarily while the threat of violence continues, and restore it once the situation calms.
Remove the post permanently and notify the lecturer, prioritising immediate safety over principle.
tension: physical safety vs. freedom of belief and criticism

title: The influencer who live-streams extreme dieting
scenario: Wellness-policy specialist Annika Lindgren at a short-video app in Sweden is examining a popular teenage influencer who documents a very low calorie diet, presenting it as discipline. Eating-disorder charities say her videos are likely to harm vulnerable viewers, while the influencer says she is recovering from earlier struggles and that the videos are her coping method. Rules ban promotion of eating disorders but allow personal stories. Annika can restrict recommendations, ask the influencer to add resources, or take no action. Her recommendation goes to a policy review on Tuesday.
options: Remove the content from recommendation feeds for under-eighteens and add a support-resource banner, leaving it accessible by search.
Remove the videos as eating-disorder promotion and offer the influencer a conversation with an eating-disorder support service.
Leave the videos unrestricted with a support banner, respecting the young woman's right to tell her own story.
tension: protecting vulnerable viewers vs. personal narrative

title: Reporting a neighbour's rumour group
scenario: Neighbourhood association volunteer Carmen Delgado in Medellin moderates a local residents' chat of two thousand people. Members share rumours naming individuals as thieves, and recently a teenager was beaten after being wrongly accused in the chat. Banning accusations altogether would prevent residents from warning each other about real crime, which is a major reason people use the group. Some residents threaten to leave for an unmoderated group. The police are rarely responsive. Carmen needs to propose new rules for the next meeting on Saturday.
options: Ban naming or showing images of suspects, allowing only descriptions of incidents and reports to police.
Require a moderator to verify any accusation before it can be posted, accepting delays in sharing urgent warnings.
Keep the current open rules but add a stern pinned reminder about false accusations, relying on residents' judgement.
tension: community safety vs. presumption of innocence

title: Scraping a hate group's recruitment forum
scenario: Researcher and part-time moderator Eilidh MacLeod in Glasgow has found that a far-right recruitment forum posts coded memes that automated filters do not recognise. She can share the coded vocabulary publicly, which would help other moderators spot the content, but it would also teach the group which terms are detected, and they might adapt. A university ethics board has told her the data is sensitive. A platform wants the list immediately after recent harassment of minority users. She must decide who gets the information and under what terms.
options: Share the vocabulary only with a closed network of trusted platform safety teams under confidentiality agreements.
Publish the vocabulary openly, trusting that wide awareness serves vulnerable communities more than secrecy.
Give the list to only the one platform that asked, keeping it out of wider circulation to preserve its usefulness.
tension: transparency vs. evasion by bad actors

title: Auto-translated insults in a cross-border gaming chat
scenario: Community lead Sakura Yamada-Ortiz manages in-game chat for a multiplayer game popular in Japan and Latin America. The auto-translation feature has turned a friendly Spanish teasing phrase into a vicious insult in Japanese and vice versa, leading to bans and tournament disputes. Disabling translation would cut off cross-cultural play, which is the game's unique feature. A top Japanese player has been banned and his fans are threatening to leave. Sakura can overturn the ban, change translation features, or hold to the current moderation rules in time for a tournament starting Sunday.
options: Overturn the ban citing the translation error, and add a notice showing the original text beside every translated message.
Uphold the ban in line with the written rules, since players are responsible for the content that appears in the chat.
Disable translation during the tournament, requiring players to use emojis and quick-chat phrases only.
tension: consistency of rules vs. fairness amid system error

title: Student-run confession page and the named teacher
scenario: Vice-principal Gideon Ndlovu in Bulawayo discovers a student-run anonymous confessions page on a social network, hosted outside the school's control. It has begun posting allegations about a specific teacher's behaviour toward pupils, some detailed. If true, the allegations are serious; if false, they could destroy a man's career. The platform will remove content on a formal school request, which would also shut down the only space where students seem willing to speak. Gideon has not yet spoken to the teacher and has no confirmation of the accounts.
options: Ask the platform to remove the posts while he opens a formal and confidential investigation, inviting students to testify safely.
Leave the page up, open an investigation, and inform the teacher without requesting its removal, keeping the students' channel intact.
Pass the allegations to the police and child-protection services, leaving them to decide on the page and the investigation.
tension: protecting students vs. presumption of innocence

title: A rape survivor's testimonial and the naming rule
scenario: Editor Beatrice Wanjala at a Ugandan women's rights site hosts a comment area where survivors share testimonies. One post names a prominent businessman as an assailant, and the site's automated tool flags it for defamation risk and hides it. The survivor says the courts will never hear her and that the post is her only recourse. The site cannot afford a defamation suit, and the businessman has threatened to sue. Beatrice can restore the post, keep it hidden, or help the survivor go to the police. She must decide before the site's weekly traffic peak.
options: Restore the post with the name intact, accepting legal risk because silencing survivors undermines the site's core mission.
Restore the post with the name redacted, and offer the survivor support to report the case through legal and advocacy channels.
Keep the post hidden, explain the reason privately to the survivor, and connect her to a lawyer and a women's legal clinic.

title: Moderation of a video of a street protest beating
scenario: News verification editor Ramon Villareal at a Philippine broadcaster's social channel receives a viral video that shows riot police beating a protester who is already on the ground. Platform AI marks it as graphic violence and limits its distribution. The video shows the faces of the officers and the victim, who has not been identified, and it could be crucial evidence of misconduct or, if edited, misleading. Ramon can't yet verify the footage's origin. The platform allows appeals for newsworthy content, but each hour of limited reach matters in the unfolding news cycle.
options: Appeal immediately for newsworthiness and publish the video with a blur on the victim's face and a note that verification is ongoing.
Hold the video until verification is complete, accepting the loss of timeliness and competition from less careful outlets.
Publish the full unedited video under the platform's graphic warning, trusting that scrutiny of police conduct outweighs privacy concerns.

title: Suppressing a rival tribe's chant at a match
scenario: Social media officer Dawit Bekele at an Ethiopian football federation manages the league's official channels, where fans post under match highlights. A chant used by one club's supporters is historically linked to a rival ethnic group and, depending on who is speaking, is either harmless tradition or taunting. Reports are growing, and auto-moderation bans the chant's words. Supporters say the ban erases their identity; opposing fans say the chant mocks past violence. A derby is coming and the federation wants calm. Dawit can write the moderation rule for the weekend.
options: Ban the chant's words in comments for the derby weekend only and publish a note explaining that the aim is calm.
Do not ban them but allow report-based removal of posts that target individuals or groups with threats or abuse.
Ban the words permanently and invite both sets of supporters to a dialogue facilitated by the federation.

title: Children's drawings flagged by the image scanner
scenario: Digital welfare officer Rina Kapoor-Hughes at a New Zealand primary school's online portal learns that the portal's image scanner flagged a pupil's drawing of a family argument as possible abuse material, triggering an automatic report to authorities that the school must review. The drawing seems to show a figure with a raised arm. The child is quiet and recently changed schools. Contacting the family could stir up trouble if there is no problem, while ignoring it risks missing real abuse. The scanner's threshold is set by the district and Rina cannot adjust it herself.
options: Speak first with the child's teacher and counsellor to gather context before deciding whether to contact the family or authorities.
Forward the report to child-protection services as the system recommends, letting trained professionals determine its significance.
Dismiss the flag as a false positive after reviewing the drawing herself, and keep a private note to watch for further signs.

title: Anonymous reviews of a rural clinic
scenario: Product manager Ngozi Eze at a Lagos-based directory of health services must decide what to do about anonymous reviews of a rural clinic. Several allege that a doctor demanded bribes for treatment, but some contain details that could identify the patients. The doctor's colleagues say the reviews are a smear by a rival. The clinic is the only one for fifty kilometres, and community leaders ask that the reviews be removed to avoid scaring patients away. The platform's policy favours keeping reviews, but she can enforce its rules about unverifiable accusations.
options: Keep the reviews, redact identifying patient details, and invite the doctor to respond publicly.
Remove the bribery allegations as unverifiable until the platform can check them, and keep all other reviews.
Keep the reviews and forward the allegations to the state medical board, trusting an official body to investigate.

title: Satirical account impersonating a mayor
scenario: Content policy analyst Anders Kjellberg-Rao in Copenhagen is reviewing a parody account of a municipal mayor, which has gained a large following by exaggerating the mayor's policy positions. Recently the posts have begun to include fabricated quotes that some residents are taking at face value, and a local newspaper repeated one. The account's label states it is parody but in small text. The mayor has asked for removal; a satire-rights group says removal would be censorship of a political critic. Anders must make a recommendation to his team before the weekend.
options: Keep the account, require a prominent parody label on every post, and remove any post found to be mistaken for real statements.
Remove the account because fabricated quotes have caused real confusion, and invite the creator to return with clearer labelling.
Keep the account unchanged, since satire is protected speech and readers should be expected to recognise exaggeration.
tension: satire and political critique vs. deception
public figure's reputation vs. free speech
